name: Electric-Assisted Bicycle
description: A bicycle with two or three wheels, a saddle, fully operative pedals and an electric motor of less than 750 watts, in one of three classes: pedal assist to 20 mph, throttle to 20 mph, or pedal assist to 28 mph.

restrictions.rule: Two or three wheels, a saddle, fully operative pedals and an electric motor of less than 750 watts
Class 1: pedal assist only, ceasing at 20 mph; Class 2: may be propelled by the motor alone, with no assistance above 20 mph; Class 3: pedal assist only, ceasing at 28 mph

One past these limits, with a motor of 750 watts or more or assisting past its class speed, isn't an electric-assisted bicycle: it's a motorized bicycle if its motor makes 3.5 brake horsepower (2,625 W) or less with an automatic transmission and a design speed of 30 mph or less, and otherwise a motor-driven cycle, titled, registered and ridden with a class M license
Riders of a Class 3 must be 16 or older; a younger passenger may ride on one designed to carry passengers
No minimum age for Class 1 or Class 2, and no statewide helmet requirement
Manufacturers must permanently affix a label stating its class, top assisted speed and motor wattage
Must not be modified to change its motor-powered speed or engagement unless the class label is replaced to match
Meets the CPSC's bicycle requirements (16 CFR part 1512)
Has the rights and duties of a bicycle and is not a motor vehicle: no driver's license, registration, title, plate or insurance
Ridden wherever bicycles are allowed, including streets, highways, bike lanes, bicycle or multi-use paths, trails and trail networks
A city may regulate it on streets and sidewalks by ordinance, and the city, county or state agency that manages a path or trail may restrict or ban it, or a single class, there
On a natural-surface trail designated nonmotorized, the local authority or state agency that manages the trail decides whether it's allowed
In state parks, only e-bikes whose assistance stops at 20 mph may use trails approved for bicycles
